key_facts: **Atypical (dysplastic) naevi** are moles that are larger (often >5 mm), irregular or variegated, but benign.
**Atypical mole syndrome**: many naevi (often >100) including several atypical ones: a strong melanoma risk factor.
**Familial melanoma**: 2 or more first-degree relatives with melanoma; CDKN2A, CDK4, BAP1 mutations; pancreatic cancer link with CDKN2A.
Manage with self-examination, total-body photography and dermoscopy surveillance, sun protection.
Refer any changing or 'ugly duckling' lesion via the suspected cancer pathway; genetics referral for familial clusters.

sections.title: Overview

ul: **Atypical (dysplastic) naevi:** clinically "funny-looking" naevi (≥5 mm, irregular or ill-defined border, variable colour, flat component. Histologically they show architectural disorder ± cytological atypia.
**Atypical mole syndrome (AMS) phenotype:** many naevi (often >100, or >50 in younger people), several atypical naevi, and naevi in unusual sites (scalp, buttocks, feet, iris).

**FAMMM** (familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome): AMS phenotype + **melanoma in ≥1–2 first- or second-degree relatives**. Germline **CDKN2A** (p16) in about 20–40% of melanoma-prone families; CDK4 is rarer. FAMMM is covered in a worked case in the [melanoma](condition:melanoma) notes too.

blocks: About 5–10% of melanomas occur in people with a family history; a smaller proportion carry a **high-penetrance germline mutation**. **FAMMM** = many (often atypical) naevi + melanoma in relatives (the [naevi](condition:melanocytic-naevi) notes see *AJCC 8th edition staging and prognosis*).

sub: Atypical naevi in about 5–10% of fair-skinned adults; inherited atypical mole syndrome is rarer.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Inherited susceptibility (CDKN2A, CDK4, MC1R variants, MITF E318K, BAP1, POT1, TERT) **plus UV**, especially intermittent intense exposure and **blistering childhood sunburn**.

ul: **"Atypical moles should all be removed"**: removal does not prevent melanoma; surveillance does detect it early.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Atypical naevi reflect a **susceptible melanocyte field** with more naevi and more mutations.

mech.t: Inherited variants (CDKN2A, MC1R, naevus-count genes) increase melanocyte proliferation.
UV and genetics produce numerous naevi, some architecturally disordered.
A lesion that differs from a person's 'signature' naevi needs assessment.
mech.caption: The ugly duckling: the lesion that looks different from the rest.

mech.t: Total-body photography and sequential dermoscopy detect change early.
mech.caption: Mole mapping: baseline photographs for comparison.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: Many naevi on the trunk and limbs, of varied sizes and colours. Look for the **"ugly duckling"**.
Early age at onset (<40), multiple primary melanomas, several affected relatives, pancreatic cancer in the family, and the AMS phenotype.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Full-skin examination, a naevus count, family history (melanoma, **pancreatic cancer**, which suggests CDKN2A), personal history, and dermoscopy. Total-body photography plus sequential digital dermoscopy (specialist).

Detailed three-generation pedigree. Refer to **clinical genetics** for germline testing (NHS National Genomic Test Directory criteria). A common UK rule of thumb: **≥3 melanomas** in an individual or family (or **2 in a high-incidence country** in some guidelines), or **melanoma + pancreatic cancer**, or melanoma + mesothelioma/uveal melanoma (BAP1).

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: Sporadic multiple melanoma
ddx.f: High UV, fair skin, no family pattern.

blocks: Common naevi in a high-naevus-count person; melanoma (individual lesion); solar lentigines (flat, sun-exposed, older).
Multiple sporadic melanomas from high UV exposure in a fair-skinned person; a common naevus phenotype.

ul: **Lifetime melanoma risk.** Each of the following raises it: Having >100 naevi (relative risk ~7); Atypical naevi; **One first-degree relative with melanoma** (about doubles the risk); **FAMMM with CDKN2A** (cumulative risk of roughly 30–70% by age 80, depending on country). The course "~15%" is a reasonable mid-range figure for AMS without a known mutation

**Refer** (routine) to dermatology for assessment: a person with an **AMS phenotype**, **≥2 first-degree relatives with melanoma**, or a personal history of melanoma. Refer to **clinical genetics** for ≥3 melanomas in the family or individual, melanoma + pancreatic cancer in the family, or multiple primary melanomas (UK cancer-genetics criteria).

**Surveillance (specialist):** total-body photography ("mole mapping") and **sequential digital dermoscopy every 3–12 months** (course teaching said 6–12) in high-risk clinics. Excise only lesions that change. **Do not prophylactically excise** atypical naevi.
**NICE NG14:** give people at increased risk **information on self-examination, sun protection and what changes to report**, and provide psychological support.

**Primary prevention:** sun protection, no sunbeds, vitamin D advice (see *Hormones, pregnancy and sunbeds*). **Children of FAMMM families** should have sun protection from birth and be examined from adolescence.

Refer the 17-year-old to **dermatology** (total-body photography plus sequential digital dermoscopy) and to **clinical genetics** (father and grandfather with early melanoma plus other family cancers).
Counsel: strict sun protection, **no sunbeds** (the under-18 ban applies to him in commercial premises), monthly self-examination, and vitamin D.

**Pancreatic cancer:** CDKN2A carriers may be offered surveillance (MRI/EUS) in research or specialist programmes, usually from 40–50 or 10 years before the youngest case. **Smoking cessation is critical** because smoking multiplies the pancreatic risk.

ladder.t: **Dermatology** (routine): AMS phenotype, **≥ 2 first-degree relatives with melanoma**, or personal melanoma (NG14). **Clinical genetics**: criteria above.
Total-body photography + **sequential digital dermoscopy every 3–12 months**; CDKN2A families: pancreatic surveillance programmes (e.g. EUROPAC).
Shade, UV clothing, hat, **SPF 30–50 reapplied every 2 h**; no sunbeds; no smoking. Outdoor workers: employer duties (HSE).
Monthly **whole-skin** checks with partner / photos: most AMS melanomas arise de novo.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Genetic testing & insurance**: UK Code: insurers can’t require predictive results (except very large policies / Huntington’s).

refer.t: Multiple atypical naevi + family history of melanoma: **dermatology surveillance**.
Melanoma and pancreatic cancer in the same family: **clinical genetics** (CDKN2A).
Any changing outlier lesion: suspected cancer pathway.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Multiple atypical naevi with a family history of melanoma: refer to a **dermatology surveillance** service (NICE NG14).
Melanoma and pancreatic cancer in the same family: refer to **clinical genetics** (CDKN2A).
Melanoma (lifetime risk greatly increased in familial disease).

pearls: The PE teacher has an outdoor occupation: shade during outdoor lessons, long-sleeved UV tops, a hat, SPF 30–50 reapplied every 2 h and after sweating. The employer has duties (HSE outdoor workers' advice).
Explain that **most melanomas in AMS arise de novo, not from existing moles**. That is why whole-skin self-checks matter more than watching one mole.

Genetic testing affects family members and insurance (UK Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance: insurers can't require predictive test results except for very large policies and Huntington's). Arrange genetic counselling before testing.
